about: The roster of the Flagships tab of the Wine Atlas (codex58), wave one: 43 classic regions in 51 groups of five producers, each with the one flagship wine a sommelier is expected to know. A group is keyed by key, titled as the page heads it, tied to its region record (region, a slug of REGIONS.regions) and its country (country, the region's sheet key in REGIONS.countries), and written by its chunk. A pick is keyed by key (unique in the plan, the seed of the record's frozen id), names the producer as the house writes it, its WINE_PRODUCERS id where the library holds the house (producerId, empty when it does not), the flagship wine (the record's wine.name holds these words, and may add the Prädikat or the style the label prints), why a sommelier is expected to know it, and, where the spec agent was unsure, a note of what the author must confirm. An author may propose a swap only with a reason and the checker's agreement: it is recorded in the group's swaps (from, to, why, agreed) and the pick replaced in the same commit. schema.cjs holds every rule; build-flagships.cjs --plan proves this file against the app. Wave two follows wave one's 51 groups in the same form: the other region records the owner chose, one group of five each, keyed by its region slug and headed as its region page is, merged from the nine lanes of plan-w2/ (kept as the record) in three batches that each ship whole once built names them, A (France, Italy, Spain, Portugal), B (Germany, Austria, Hungary, Greece) and C (the New York sheet, Argentina, Chile, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa), each group carrying its batch and its chunk of wave two (w1 on, three groups a chunk in plan order, never two batches in one); a region whose lane could not source five houses waits in plan-w2/ and joins the plan only when five are sourced, since a group never ships short.

The record must say it is a co-operative.

picks.why: Getaria family house on the slopes above the sea, among the growers of the Getariako Txakolina DO of 1989; its white of Hondarrabi Zuri is the classic Getaria txakoli, poured from a height.

Confirm its part in the DO of 1989, the family's history (records of the seventeenth century are told) and the label from two sources; name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Getaria family house with vineyards above the sea; Rubentis, its rosado of Hondarrabi Beltza with Hondarrabi Zuri, is the pink face of Getaria the region record names the house for.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this lane. Confirm the blend, that Rubentis is a Getariako Txakolina rosado, the family's history and any founding year from two sources; name no living member of the family. The house's white is the other wine.

picks.why: Gernika house of 1995 in the Bizkaiko Txakolina DO, with whites of Hondarrabi Zuri, some kept on their lees; Itsasmendi 7 is its fuller white, made to stand beside the Basque table.

picks.why: Bakio estate, a reference for Bizkaia's txakoli; Gorrondona, its white of Hondarrabi Zuri with a little Hondarrabi Beltza, is the house's wine to know, and its rare red of Hondarrabi Beltza is the region's other face.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirm the white's blend from two sources and that Gorrondona is its name on the label (Doniene is the lees aged white); by one source the red was renamed Beltza from the 2018 vintage. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Okondo estate in the Ayala valley of Álava, its first harvest in 2007, and a reference for Arabako Txakolina, the youngest of the three DOs; Astobiza is its white txakoli of the inland valley.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The sources give 2006 and 2007 for the founding (first harvest 2007): confirm from two or leave founded empty. Confirm the label (Astobiza, sold as Señorío de Astobiza) and its grapes (Hondarrabi Zuri, with Izkiriota told for some bottlings); Malkoa is its single plot white and the Izkiriota late harvest its sweet.

picks.why: O Bolo house of 2004 in the Bibei valley of Valdeorras, Godello on decomposed granite fermented and aged in large wood; As Sortes is the wine the library says established Godello as a fine white grape.
picks.note: The house is named for a living man of the Palacios family, so the prose says the house, never him; Descendientes de J. Palacios, a pick of this lane, and wave one's Priorat house are other houses of the family. Confirm the label (As Sortes, Valdeorras) and its parcels.

picks.why: Valdeorras family estate whose Guitián Godello, kept on its lees or fermented in barrel, is the wine the region record says helped make the grape's name.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this lane: confirm the house, its village and founding year, and the label (Guitián Godello Sobre Lías and Guitián Fermentado en Barrica are told: choose the one taught) from two sources; name no living member of the family. Godeval, of the monastery of Xagoaza, is the alternative with the checker's agreement.

picks.why: Doade house of the Amandi subzone, terracing the canyon of the Sil, and one of the founding wineries of the Ribeira Sacra DO of 1996; Pizarra, Spanish for slate, is its Mencía of the terraces.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The founding year differs by source (1980, the 1990s, 2005): leave founded empty unless two agree. Confirm that Pizarra is the flagship (the sources list it among the reds and none calls it the flagship) and its grapes; Merenzao and Brancellao are the house's native grape reds. The family are living, never named.

picks.why: Estate of the Bibei valley in Quiroga-Bibei, the region record's house for Mencía led reds and Godello from steep terraces; Lalama is its red of Mencía with native grapes beside it.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this lane: confirm the house, the label (Lalama, Ribeira Sacra), its grapes (Mencía with Brancellao, Mouratón and Garnacha Tintorera are told), the founding year and Lacima as the house's other red from two sources.

picks.why: The trading name of Ribeiro's co-operative at Ribadavia, founded by its growers in 1968; Viña Costeira, a white led by Treixadura, is the Ribeiro many guests meet first.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The co-operative's name is Vitivinícola del Ribeiro: confirm it and 1968 (its Colección 68 is named for the year) from two sources. Confirm the white's blend for the years taught; the record must say it is a co-operative.

picks.why: The Melgaço family estate that bottled the first Alvarinho of the municipality in 1982, by its own account, and whose Alvarinho carried the subregion's grape abroad.

picks.why: The Monção manor whose varietal Alvarinho, sold from the 1970s, made the grape's name in Portugal before most growers bottled it.
picks.note: Confirm the first vintage (1976 by report), the manor's building and its purchase in 1937 in two sources; name the woman who planted the Alvarinho only if two sources give her dates and her death.

picks.why: The Melgaço house of a winemaker who showed Alvarinho could take lees, skin contact and oak; Muros Antigos is its wide release Alvarinho, the bottle a list carries.
picks.note: The founder is living: the house keeps its name and he is never named in prose. Confirm Muros Antigos's making; Curtimenta and Parcela Única go in others.

picks.why: The Penafiel house of the Guedes family behind Casal Garcia, launched in 1939, the light, lightly sparkling Vinho Verde that carried the region's name abroad.
picks.note: Confirm the 1939 launch and the blend in words (Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto and Azal by report) from Aveleda's page; the family's living members are never named.

picks.why: The Lima valley estate that showed Loureiro, the Lima's own grape, could be made seriously and age; Esporão bought it in 2019.
picks.note: Confirm the label (Quinta do Ameal Loureiro, Ameal Loureiro since 2019) and the estate's history before 2019 in two sources; the former owner is living and is never named; the Reserva of the Marinhas plot goes in others.

picks.why: A family estate at Abrunhosa do Mato between Mangualde and Nelas whose varietal Touriga Nacional and barrel-fermented Encruzado helped define the modern Dão in the 1990s.
picks.note: Confirm the first varietal Touriga Nacional and its year in two sources; the family is living and is never named; the Encruzado goes in others.

picks.why: The old-vine estate under the Serra da Estrela near Seia, with its sister Quinta de Saes, whose fine-boned reds argue for the Dão's elegance; Carrocel, its Touriga Nacional from old vines, is the estate's flagship.
picks.note: The library's record is Álvaro Castro (Quinta da Pellada and Quinta de Saes): the winemaker is living, so the house is named by its estate and he is never named in prose. Confirm Carrocel's label and grapes; Primus and Pape go in others, Pape without its living partner's name.

picks.why: Sogrape's Dão estate at Mangualde and a reference for Encruzado, the Dão's white grape, fermented partly in new oak; Único, the estate's red, is its other face.
picks.note: Confirm the Encruzado's making from Sogrape's own sheet and the year Sogrape took the estate in two sources; Único goes in others.

picks.why: The historic manor of Santar near Nelas, among the first houses to bottle estate Dão; its Reserva red of Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz is the wine a list carries.
picks.note: Sources disagree on the manor's age (sixteenth to eighteenth century): leave founded empty unless two agree; confirm the early estate bottling and the Reserva's grapes in words; the Condessa de Santar white goes in others.

picks.why: A nineteenth century estate at Passarella near Gouveia under the Serra da Estrela, revived with its old vines; Villa Oliveira, its Touriga Nacional from an old vineyard, is its flagship red.
picks.note: Confirm the building of 1892 (one source) and the age of the Villa Oliveira vineyard in two sources; those who revived it are living and are never named; the Villa Oliveira Encruzado goes in others.

picks.why: The Anadia house that championed Baga from the 1980s with single-vineyard wines; Vinha Barrosa, from old bush vines, is the traditional face of the grape, and the ungrafted Pé Franco on sand its rarity.
picks.note: The founder is living: the house keeps its name and he is never named in prose. Confirm Vinha Barrosa's soils and the label's category (Vinho Regional, the house having left the DOC, by report); the Pé Franco and Vinha Pan go in others.

picks.why: The Bairrada merchant house founded in 1920 by the Costa brothers, whose Frei João reds, kept for years in its cellars before release, showed how long Baga could live.
picks.note: Name the brothers only with dates from two sources; confirm which Frei João to teach (Reserva or Garrafeira) and its grapes; Porta dos Cavaleiros, the house's Dão, goes in others.

picks.why: A family estate near Anadia making Baga the old way, in lagar and old wood, and sparkling wine with long lees ageing; its Garrafeira red is the classic Bairrada to know.
picks.note: Confirm the Garrafeira's label and making in two sources; the family is living and is never named; the sparkling wines go in others.

picks.why: A Sangalhos estate making Baga in the old manner, trodden in lagar and aged in old wood, whose Garrafeira red shows the slow-ageing classic style of the region.
picks.note: Confirm the estate's history and dates and the Garrafeira's making in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: The palace hotel in the Buçaco forest whose red and white, blended from Bairrada and Dão grapes and aged for years before release, are sold as table wine outside both appellations.
picks.note: Confirm the label words (Buçaco Tinto Reservado, Vinho de Mesa) and the old cellar's vintages in two sources; the hotel's family and any living winemaker or partner are never named.

picks.why: The co-operative founded in 1931 that keeps Colares alive, ageing Ramisco from ungrafted vines in the sand by the sea in old vats for years before release.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year and any claim of Portugal's oldest wine co-operative only in two sources; confirm Arenae's label (Colares, Ramisco) and its ageing.

picks.why: A Colares house dating from 1808 by its own account, whose cellar of old vintages shows how Ramisco from the sand ages over decades.
picks.note: Hedge 1808 as the house's claim and confirm the red's label wording (Colares, Ramisco) in two sources; the living owners are never named; the Malvasia white goes in others.

picks.why: The Bucelas estate whose Prova Régia, all Arinto, made the white-only appellation's grape known abroad; the name recalls royal approval.
picks.note: One listing gives Sogrape as the maker: confirm who has made Prova Régia and since when before writing ownership; the estate is spelled Romeyra on some labels; Morgado de Santa Catherina goes in others.

picks.why: The project of the Oeiras municipal council that brought Carcavelos, the fortified wine of the coast west of Lisbon, back from near extinction, and almost the only maker of the appellation.
picks.note: Confirm the project's start, the vineyard it farms and the ages on its labels in two sources; the Marquis of Pombal (1699 to 1782) may be named with his dates.

picks.why: The Alenquer estate that proved Syrah belongs in Lisboa; its Reserva, Syrah with a little Viognier in the manner of the northern Rhône, is the house's flagship.
picks.note: Sources disagree on the estate's start (bought in 1987 with a first wine in 1997, or founded in 1990): leave founded empty unless two agree; the founder is living and is never named.

picks.why: An Almeirim estate dating from 1723, named for a marquisate won in India, and one of the Tejo's oldest names; the Marquesa de Alorna Grande Reserva is its flagship range.
picks.note: Confirm 1723 and the marquisate's story from the estate or two sources; the Grande Reserva is made red and white, so the author names the colour taught and its grapes.

picks.why: An old family estate at Almeirim whose Falcoaria label, named for the house's falconry, carries the Tejo's firmer reds of traditional grapes and oak-aged whites.
picks.note: Confirm the falconry story and which Falcoaria to teach (the red, or the Grande Reserva) in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: The Muge estate on the left bank of the Tejo, held by one family for centuries, whose Marquesa de Cadaval red is its flagship.
picks.note: Confirm the founding (1648 by one retailer) and the family's history in two sources; labels write de or do Cadaval and a white of the name exists, so name the red's grapes only as the estate states them; the Trincadeira Preta goes in others.

picks.why: A large estate at Alpiarça on the south bank that grows Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Syrah beside horses and cork; its Grande Escolha reds, bottled by grape, show the modern Tejo on one farm.
picks.note: The Grande Escolha is bottled as Syrah and as Alfrocheiro: choose one and name it whole on the record from the estate's sheet; the Dona Isabel Juliana sparkling goes in others.

picks.why: The farm company of the floodplain founded in 1836, whose winery at Catapereiro on the Charneca sand shows what the south bank can do when yields are held down; its 1836 range carries the founding year.
picks.note: Confirm the 1836 range's label and colour (a Grande Reserva white is recorded) in two sources; the Tyto Alba range, from vines in the estuary's nature reserve, goes in others.

picks.why: The Azeitão house founded in 1834 that made Moscatel de Setúbal its name, its Moscatel brand dating from 1849 by its own timeline; Alambre is its Moscatel, and Periquita, of 1850, its red.
picks.note: Not the Port house of the same name. Confirm which Alambre to teach (the young one or the 20 Anos) and the Torna Viagem story from the house's own pages; Periquita goes in others.

picks.why: The Azeitão company, once J.P. Vinhos, named for the palace and estate of Bacalhôa, whose Quinta da Bacalhôa, a red of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, is its flagship.
picks.note: Confirm the first vintage of the Quinta da Bacalhôa red and the vineyard's planting from the company or two sources; the company's living owner is never named; the Moscatels and Palácio da Bacalhôa go in others.

picks.why: A family estate at Fernando Pó on the Palmela sand, dating from 1920 by report, that built its name on Castelão; Dona Ermelinda is its Palmela red.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year, the Dona Ermelinda red's appellation (Palmela) and its grapes in two sources; the living family is never named.

picks.why: A family house of the peninsula dating from 1910 by report, credited with bringing back Moscatel Roxo, the pink-skinned Muscat once near lost, as fortified Moscatel de Setúbal.
picks.note: Confirm 1910 and the revival claim in two sources, and the label (Moscatel de Setúbal Roxo and its age statement); the living family is never named.

picks.why: The co-operative of the Pegões plain, the everyday voice of the peninsula's wine; its Colheita Seleccionada, made red and white, is its widely seen label.
picks.note: Confirm the colour taught (the white is Fernão Pires, Antão Vaz, Verdelho, Arinto and Chardonnay by one sheet), the co-operative's full name and founding; its Moscatel goes in others.

picks.why: The traditional Alentejo in one estate: Alicante Bouschet planted since the nineteenth century, trodden in stone lagares and aged in old wood; Mouchão, its red made only in accepted years, lasts for decades.
picks.note: Name members of the founding family only with dates from two sources; confirm the years Mouchão was not made; Tonel 3-4 goes in others.

picks.why: The Évora foundation that makes wine at Cartuxa beside the Carthusian monastery that named it, and bottles Pêra-Manca red only in the years it judges fit.
picks.note: Name the founder only with dates from two sources; confirm the red's first vintage and tell the older story of the Pêra-Manca name as legend where it is one; Cartuxa Reserva goes in others.

picks.why: The Reguengos estate whose winery of the 1980s led the Alentejo's modern revival; its Reserva red is one of the region's widely known wines.
picks.note: Confirm the founding, the first Reserva vintage and the red's grapes in words in two sources; the founding family is living and is never named; the white Reserva goes in others.

picks.why: The co-operative of the marble country, founded in 1955, whose Reserva red with its cork label taught a generation of Portuguese what an Alentejo red tastes like.
picks.note: Confirm the founding year and the cork label (rótulo de cortiça) in two sources, and the Reserva's grapes in words.

picks.why: A Vidigueira estate whose Syrah, first released in 1998, could not be named for its grape under the rules of the day and was sold as Incógnito; Syrah has since been admitted.
picks.note: Confirm 1998 and the year of the rule change in two sources; the founders are living and are never named; the label is Vinho Regional Alentejano.

picks.why: Dernau family estate on the valley's steep slate, a house of the turn to dry, barrel aged Spätburgunder in the 1980s; the Pfarrwingert is its Grosses Gewächs, the Ahr's red in one glass.
picks.note: Confirm the label's form for the years taught (Dernauer Pfarrwingert or Dernau Pfarrwingert) and date the dry turn only from two sources; the Walporzheimer Kräuterberg GG goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Rech family estate of the middle valley; the Herrenberg, a steep slope of slate above the village and a VDP Grosse Lage, gives its Spätburgunder Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The sources disagree on the house's age (winemaking from 1578 in one, a winery since 1900 in another): leave founded empty unless two agree. Confirm the soil of the site and the oak regime from the house; name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Ahrweiler family estate that holds the whole of the Gärkammer at Walporzheim, which the VDP calls the smallest of its Grosse Lagen in Germany, planted to Spätburgunder alone and named, the VDP says, for the heat it holds in summer.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The VDP's own pages are the primary for the monopole, its size among the Grosse Lagen and the name; confirm the label's form (Walporzheimer or Walporzheim Gärkammer) and name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Mayschoss estate of the upper valley, a VDP house making Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder; the Mönchberg above the village, a Grosse Lage, gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Decanter dates the estate's records to 1574 and a wine encyclopedia calls it the Mönchberg's largest holder: give either only with a second source. Confirm the label's form; name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Dernau family estate known for Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder; its Grosses Gewächs of Spätburgunder comes from the Hardtberg at Dernau, so the group shows Dernau's second Grosse Lage beside Meyer-Näkel's Pfarrwingert.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Decanter names the Hardtberg GG as the house's own and dates the estate to 1953: confirm both in a second source and the label's form. The Mayschoss cooperative of 1868, the oldest in Germany by the region record, is the valley's history and may be told in a story, not a pick.

picks.why: Oberhausen family estate of 1750 by the library's date, which carried the Nahe onto lists abroad; the Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen gives its dry Grosses Gewächs, and the library teaches the site as a wine of its own.
picks.note: The library also holds the site as w-hermannshohle: tie the record to p-donnhoff. Confirm 1750 in two sources, the site's soils before naming them, and the label's form; the sweet Oberhäuser Brücke Spätlese from the house's monopole goes in others.

picks.why: Monzingen family estate of the upper Nahe; the Halenberg, a steep slope of blue slate and quartzite by the library's account, gives its Grosses Gewächs, with the Frühlingsplätzchen beside it.
picks.note: Confirm the Halenberg's soils in two sources and the label's form for the years taught; the Halenberg Auslese goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Bockenau family estate in a side valley of the Nahe, fermenting with wild yeasts into a smoky, struck match style; the Felseneck above the village gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Confirm the Felseneck's soil before naming it and the label's form; the house also holds Kupfergrube and Felsenberg, so say which goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Niederhausen estate founded by the Prussian state in 1902 as its Nahe domain, on steep rocky ground that took in an abandoned copper mine; the Kupfergrube, planted on the mine, gives its Grosses Gewächs.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The Wines of Germany page is the national body's account of the domain: confirm 1902 and the mine's working until 1901 in a second source, tell the sale of 2009 as history with no living name, and confirm whether the house still holds the GG back for a later release.

picks.why: Burg Layen family estate of the lower Nahe, known for Riesling from Dorsheim's Goldloch, Pittermännchen and Burgberg and for its traditional method Sekt; the Goldloch is its Grosses Gewächs to know.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm in two sources that the Goldloch GG leads the house's range rather than the Pittermännchen or the Burgberg, the label's form, and the Sekt for others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Flörsheim-Dalsheim family estate of the Wonnegau, of 1789 by the library's date, whose dry Rieslings from limestone changed what Rheinhessen meant; G-Max is its dry Riesling from old vines with no site on the label, a wine the library holds on its own.
picks.note: The library also holds the wine as w-g-max: tie the record to p-keller. Confirm in two sources what the house says of G-Max (its first vintage, the parcels, the story of its name) and teach it with nothing that dates. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Westhofen family estate farmed organically and then biodynamically; the Morstein, limestone of the Wonnegau, gives its Grosses Gewächs, the same site as Keller's read in a rounder house style.
picks.note: Confirm the label's form (Westhofener or Westhofen Morstein) and the date of the biodynamic turn in two sources; Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Aulerde go in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Nackenheim estate of 1890 by the library's date, on the Roter Hang; the Rothenberg, the red slate cliff above the Rhine, gives its dry Grosses Gewächs and sweet wines up to Trockenbeerenauslese.
picks.note: Confirm 1890 in two sources and the label's form; the Rothenberg Trockenbeerenauslese goes in others. Name no living member of the family.

picks.why: Bodenheim family estate working the red slope's Pettenthal, Hipping, Ölberg and Rothenberg; its Grosses Gewächs from the Pettenthal at Nierstein shows the Roter Hang's smoky, stony Riesling.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own material puts the Rothenberg wurzelecht, from ungrafted vines, forward as its signature: the Pettenthal is chosen so the page does not show the Rothenberg twice beside Gunderloch, and the author may propose the swap with the checker's agreement. The estate is run with Battenfeld-Spanier by one couple: say so with no names, or leave it out. Merge read: the owner asked for each house's own flagship, so the spread of a page is never a reason to teach a lesser wine; if the house's own pages set the Rothenberg wurzelecht first, swap to it with the checker, since two Rothenbergs on one page are two houses and no repeat.

picks.why: Hohen-Sülzen family estate in the far south of the Wonnegau, farmed biodynamically on limestone; its Grosses Gewächs from the Frauenberg at Nieder-Flörsheim is the cool, chalky side of the region.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Meininger's tastings put the Frauenberg forward and the house's own material the Zellerweg am Schwarzen Herrgott: confirm in two sources which leads, and the label's form; the Kirchenstück goes in others.

picks.why: Escherndorf family estate above a bend of the Main; its dry Silvaner Grosses Gewächs comes from Am Lumpen 1655, the heart of the steep Lump, and teaches the grape that defines the region.
picks.note: The library writes Escherndorfer Lump Silvaner GG; Falstaff and the house's importer print Am Lumpen 1655: confirm the label's form and that 1655 is the site's first mention, in two sources. Keep the house apart from Weingut Rainer Sauer, a separate Escherndorf estate whose wine from the same site carries the same name. The Lump Trockenbeerenauslese goes in others.

picks.why: Würzburg charitable foundation of 1576 whose vineyards have long paid for its hospital; its Silvaner Grosses Gewächs comes from the Stein, the shell limestone slope above the city that gave Steinwein its name.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS and not searched in this run: confirm 1576 and the founder, Prince Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn, with his dates, in two sources, and that the Stein rather than the Iphöfer Julius-Echter-Berg is the house's lead Silvaner.

picks.why: Würzburg charitable foundation of 1316, the older of the city's two; the Stein-Harfe, a Grosse Lage within the Stein in its sole ownership, gives its Silvaner Grosses Gewächs, while its Stein-Harfe Rieslings are sweet.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own pages are the primary for the Stein-Harfe; confirm 1316 and its founder in two sources. The sweet Stein-Harfe Riesling Spätlese goes in others.

picks.why: Bürgstadt family estate of the Mainviereck on red sandstone, the red side of Franken; the Hundsrück is the Grosse Lage of its Spätburgunder, beside the Centgrafenberg.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirm in two sources that the Hundsrück rather than the Centgrafenberg is the house's lead Spätburgunder, when it was first bottled alone, and the label's form; the Frühburgunder and the Centgrafenberg go in others. Give the house's namesake dates only from two sources, and name no living member of the family.

picks.why: The princely Castell estate of the Steigerwald, on gypsum Keuper; the Schlossberg below the castle gives its Silvaner Grosses Gewächs, and the house tells of the first Silvaner recorded in Germany, planted at Castell in April 1659.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Confirm the planting of 6 April 1659 in two sources (the house's own page counts for its own claim, hedged), whether the Schlossberg is held alone, and how the house writes its name; tell the princely family's history with no living name.

picks.why: Schwaigern estate of the counts of Neipperg, a family that has championed Lemberger for generations; the Ruthe is the Grosse Lage of its Lemberger Grosses Gewächs, with the Schlossberg beside it.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. The house's own wine list names the Ruthe Lemberger GG; confirm the family's history in two sources and keep its tie to a Saint-Émilion estate as history only, with no living name.

picks.why: Fellbach family estate on the edge of Stuttgart; its Riesling Grosses Gewächs from Gips Marienglas, a parcel of gypsum Keuper at Untertürkheim, shows the white side of a red region.
picks.note: Not in WINE_PRODUCERS. Falstaff lists both this wine and the Fellbacher Lämmler Lemberger GG the region record names: the Riesling is chosen for the group's spread, and the author may argue for the Lämmler with the checker. Confirm that Marienglas names the gypsum crystal of the soil, and the label's form.
